On the last Thursday before the bridge came down, the city sent a woman to record it.

Her name was Mara, and she worked in an office that usually recorded things nobody noticed until they stopped working: the warning bell at the reservoir, the hum of the old courthouse elevators, the tone played before announcements at the bus station.

“Why the bridge?” she asked her supervisor.

“It makes a noise,” he said.

Everything made a noise, but Mara had learned that this was not an argument worth having.

She arrived at nine with a microphone, a recorder, and a thermos of tea. The bridge crossed a narrow river that looked, from that height, like a strip of unpolished metal. Beyond it stood the new bridge: wider, brighter, and already carrying most of the traffic.

The old one creaked when the wind moved through its joints. It gave a low, hollow boom when a truck crossed. Each footstep set off a small chain of clicks beneath the pavement, like someone running a stick along a fence.

Mara was recording these when a man stopped beside her.

“Are you looking for the bird?” he asked.

“I’m recording the bridge.”

“Oh,” he said. “You’ll get the bird too, then.”

He was carrying a paper bag darkened at the bottom by grease. He set it on the railing and took out a pastry.

“What bird?” Mara asked.

The man pointed to a streetlamp halfway across the bridge. “There’s a starling that does the crossing signal.”

They waited. Traffic murmured from the new bridge. A cyclist passed behind them, and the old bridge clicked.

Then, from the streetlamp, came a clear mechanical chirp: *peep-peep, peep-peep.*

It was followed by a sound like a car alarm losing confidence.

“There,” the man said.

Mara turned the microphone toward the lamp. The bird performed the crossing signal twice more, then tried a few notes of something she couldn’t identify.

“My wife used to bring it crumbs,” the man said. “We’d walk over after her appointments.”

“At the hospital?”

He nodded. “She liked to stop here on the way back. Said she wanted to arrive home as a different person from the one who’d left.”

He broke a piece from the pastry and put it on the railing. The starling flew down, inspected it, and returned to the lamp.

“Not hungry,” he said. “Or doesn’t like lemon.”

They stood for a while. Mara watched the levels rise and fall on her recorder.

“Is your wife still in the hospital?” she asked.

“No. She died in February.”

“I’m sorry.”

He nodded, as if confirming a date in a diary. He brushed sugar from his fingers and picked up the paper bag.

Before leaving, he asked what would happen to the recording.

“It goes into the city archive,” Mara said. “People can request a copy.”

“Will anyone?”

“Sometimes they do.”

At the office, she listened through headphones. There was the groan of the girders, the truck’s boom, the long wash of tires on the new bridge. And there was the starling, reproducing the crossing signal so exactly that Mara glanced up from her desk, half expecting the little green figure to appear.

She filed the recording under *Infrastructure: Bridges, Eastbank*. Then she made a second copy and labeled it *Starling on bridge*. She put the man’s description in the notes, though she did not know his name.

Three weeks later, the bridge was gone. Mara took her lunch down to the river and sat where she could see the new one. It had smooth railings and lamps shaped like white teardrops. A cyclist crossed without making a sound she could hear.

She had nearly finished eating when a starling landed on the bench beside her.

It regarded her sandwich.

“Not hungry,” Mara told it.

The bird tilted its head. Then it made the long, flat beep of a reversing vehicle, and she laughed loudly enough that someone across the path turned around.

She tore off a bit of bread and set it on the bench. This time, the bird took it.
